note: Seven parties touch a hardening rule between the body that writes it and the auditor who reads the outcome, and each one works in an OSCAL model. Which model is the whole of what an approach asks of a party, so this is a mapping rather than an argument. Two entries need their component type named, because the same model does two jobs for two different parties. Two sets of the seven are grouped. The bodies that author hardening guidance are one role played by two kinds of organisation. The automation is a policy engine and the two parties that run it: a provider builds the tool and runs nothing, which is why its flows name whoever executes them, and the system owner and the auditor are those parties. The mapping provider is a party of its own because a hardening guide does not always carry the tie to a framework: a STIG carries CCIs and it is DISA's separate CCI list that names the 800-53 controls, and third parties publish mappings of their own through NIST's OLIR programme. Whoever writes the guide is often not whoever ties it to the framework.
intro: Seven parties touch a hardening rule between a published guide and an audited system, and each works in an OSCAL model. Two sets of them are grouped: the bodies that author guidance, and the automation.

parties.name: Regulatory control providers
parties.who: NIST with SP 800-53, and bodies like it

parties.name: Mapping providers
parties.who: DISA's CCI list, NIST's OLIR programme, the Secure Controls Framework and bodies like them, tying a guide to a framework

parties.name: Technical hardening guidance providers
parties.who: CIS, DISA and other benchmark publishers

parties.name: Software providers
parties.who: Vendors publishing secure configuration guidance for their own product, alone or with a body such as CIS

parties.name: Policy engine providers
parties.who: OPA, Kyverno, ScubaGear, OpenSCAP and the like, assessing, auditing and checking

parties.name: System owners
parties.who: Implementing these concepts on a real system

parties.name: Independent auditors
parties.who: Running the same checks independently of the system owner, and reading the outcome

mapper.note: The one approach where the tie is a document of its own, and the mapping provider's to write. No publisher has shipped one for hardening guidance yet.

engine.note: Builds the tool and runs nothing. What it ships is the check, as a component of type software. The catalog it points at is the guidance authors'.

owner.note: The profile is always the owner's: the selection of what this system is held to, and the merge of the catalogs a plan can import.

auditor.note: The same checks, a different party running them. What comes out is a result, and its finding targets the statement the owner wrote.

mapper.note: Edits a definition rather than writing one. Which of the two carries the tie, the rules or the checks, is an open question.

engine.note: A component of type validation rather than software, holding the checks. Builds it, runs nothing.

auditor.note: The run goes through the assessment plan, which is what lets the result name the host rather than the component.

mapper.note: Edits the plan rather than writing one. Reviewed-controls on the activity names the framework controls the check covers.

benchmark.note: Writes the activity and its steps. The check that runs them is the engine's.

software.note: Writes the activity and its steps. The check that runs them is the engine's.

engine.note: The plan is the engine's, and the checks in it are what it adds. It is named inside the plan too, in assessment-assets.

owner.note: The selection and the plan of record, and nothing beyond them. An assessor's run takes no dependency on what the owner automates, and cannot see it.

auditor.note: The only run here. There is no path from a check to a claim, so what comes out is a result and never the plan of record.

groups.label: Hardening guidance authors
groups.note: One role, two kinds of organisation, the same model. Nothing downstream can tell which of them wrote a rule.

groups.label: Automation tools and who runs them
groups.note: The policy engine and the automation tool are the same thing. A provider builds it, and whoever runs it decides what comes out.

runtime: A tool reads OSCAL, executes, and writes OSCAL. The party in this row builds it; the party on each flow runs it.
